description: How chairs, rope and lighting transform into trains, ships and continents on a bare stage.
content_html:
Designing a World Without a Set

Eason’s stage adaptation was conceived for theatre in the round at the New Vic, Newcastle-under-Lyme. That original configuration shapes every design decision: there is no back wall to hang flats on, no single “front” to place a painted landscape. Everything must work from all angles. This forces the production into a minimalist aesthetic where objects, light and bodies carry the entire scenic burden — and that turns out to be the production’s greatest creative asset.

For a GCSE Drama student, this unit is a masterclass in how minimal scenography can actually communicate more than a fully realised naturalistic set. When the audience watches the company convert four chairs into a railway carriage, they are not passive observers — they are actively co-creating the fiction. The designer’s job is to give them just enough information so that their imagination completes the picture.

Key Fact

The production typically uses chairs as railway carriages, rope as ship rigging and canes as multiple tools — each transformation is achieved through precise physical use by the performer, not through visual trickery.

Set Design: The Empty Space as Possibility

The set designer’s first decision is stage configuration and levels. A production of this play that uses a central raised platform for the Reform Club gives Fogg an immediate visual authority: he is literally above the world he is about to conquer. When Passepartout operates at floor level, the contrast in levels communicates their relationship instantly, before a word is spoken.

Across the episodic structure, the only constants are a table and a set of chairs that can be reconfigured per scene. A row of chairs placed upstage and angled slightly can become the viewing gallery of the Reform Club; the same chairs rotated and placed downstage become a train carriage hurtling across America. The speed of these reconfigurations is part of the show’s theatrical language — an audience that sees chairs moved quickly learns to read those moves as scene changes and accepts the new location immediately.

A persistent student misconception is to suggest a large scenic elephant as the design solution for the India sequence. This misses the form the play is written for. Productions use puppet elephants or pure physical theatre (ensemble bodies) precisely because the play’s style is anti-naturalistic. Suggesting a painted or mechanised elephant in an exam answer signals that you have misread the genre. Examiners reward students who suggest stylised physical solutions consistent with the ensemble aesthetic — for example, a puppet elephant built collaboratively by the company using poles, fabric and collective movement, or pure ensemble mime.

Lighting Design: Painting the Globe

Because the set is minimal, the lighting designer carries enormous scenic responsibility. Each new location must be painted in light. A warm amber wash from a high angle creates the heat of India; a cold blue wash from the sides suggests the Atlantic crossing in winter; a neutral, slightly grey top light places us in foggy London. Lighting wash choices are the quickest way to transport an audience across continents.

More specific effects come from lantern choices. A profile lantern can be used to throw a hard-edged spotlight onto Fogg at the moment of the wager — isolating him from the Reform Club chatter as if the rest of the world has receded. A gobo of moving water patterns projected from above transforms the bare stage floor into the surface of the ocean for the Atlantic crossing. These specific design choices communicate location and mood simultaneously without a single piece of scenery being added.

Key Fact

Lighting transitions replace scene changes in this production. The move from a warm amber wash (India) to a cold blue wash (the Atlantic) is a design shorthand that takes less than ten seconds and instantly relocates the audience without a single piece of furniture being moved.

Sound Design: A Soundscape Around the World

The soundscape is equally important. Train whistles, steam hiss, ship bells, the call to prayer from a minaret, Yokohama street noise and the rhythmic clatter of railway track can all be designed into the production’s score. The sound designer has two main tools: diegetic sounds (those the characters would hear — the steam engine’s release of pressure) and non-diegetic underscore (a rising orchestral phrase as Fogg’s train accelerates, unheard by Fogg but felt by the audience).

Some productions interpolate live music — a pianist in the corner, a percussionist tracking the journey — which adds the additional layer of music-hall theatricality that the play’s comic tradition invites. The sound of a music-hall piano underscoring a chase sequence immediately signals that the play is aware of its own genre and inviting the audience to enjoy the theatricality, not just the story.

Costume Design: Identity in an Accessory

Costume design in this production must solve the multi-roling problem: one performer will play many roles, so each role must be instantly readable from a limited set of accessories. The base layer — typically a neutral Victorian-inflected suit in grey or cream — stays constant. Over it, a pith helmet signals India; a captain’s peaked cap and a slightly maritime posture signals the ship; a sheepskin hat and heavier coat signals the American West.

Signifier costume strategy means the designer must choose accessories that read clearly from every audience sightline (critical in in-the-round staging) and that can be donned and shed in seconds. The choice of colour is also important for character identity: Fogg’s costume is typically a consistent, precise dark grey or navy — the visual equivalent of his personality. Passepartout, by contrast, might have a slightly more bohemian base layer and brighter accessories to signal his continental exuberance.

As a lighting designer for the moment when the company begins burning the ship’s wooden deck for fuel, you might build from a cool steel-blue wash (open Atlantic, night-time) and introduce a warm orange-red flicker from below stage level — using floor-level lanterns or footlights — to suggest the growing fire. The juxtaposition of cold blue above and warm orange below creates a visual instability that mirrors the desperation of the moment. A slow, pulsing rhythm to the flicker (rather than a frantic strobe) keeps the audience in the drama rather than pulling them into a safety-concern.

As a sound designer, you might layer a low, continuous drone beneath the scene — representing the ship’s engines slowing — with the distant crack and hiss of timber burning. Non-diegetic underscore could begin quietly here: a single, sustained string note that rises very gradually in pitch as the fire takes hold, cueing the audience that something important is at stake without spelling it out.
exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark designer question, the most frequent error is to give one vague idea per discipline (“I would use interesting lighting”) without naming specific elements or explaining their effect. You must name the lantern type (profile, Fresnel, flood, gobo), the colour or gel, the direction and the effect it creates for the audience at that exact moment. For this play in particular, remember that the minimal set means light is doing the job of scenery — your lighting choices are location choices as well as mood choices. For the 20-mark extended staging response, cover all four design disciplines (set, lighting, sound, costume) AND performer choices, anchoring every point to the named moment in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Minimal scenography is a creative strength, not a limitation: the audience co-creates each location, lighting transitions replace scene changes, and every design choice carries double duty (mood and geography simultaneously).
  • Lighting is the primary scenic tool in this production — wash colours, gobos and profile lanterns each communicate a specific geographic location or emotional state without a single piece of scenery being added.
  • Costume design uses a signifier strategy: a base layer plus rapidly changed accessories lets multi-roling performers shift character in seconds while maintaining consistent identity for the principal characters.

practice_questions.text: Name the staging configuration in which the original New Vic production of Around the World in 80 Days was performed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: theatre in the round (accept in-the-round).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'minimal scenography' as it applies to this production.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that minimal scenography uses as few physical set elements as possible; 1 mark for explaining that lighting, sound and performance substitute for physical scenery, creating location through non-material means.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a lighting designer might use a warm amber wash and a gobo to create the atmosphere of the India sequence. Refer to the specific effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: naming the warm amber wash and its association with heat and sunlight (1); naming the gobo and the specific pattern it would project (leaf shadow, sun dapple) (1); explaining the effect of the combination on the audience's sense of location (instant geographical orientation without set) (1); explaining the emotional or thematic effect (warmth, exoticism, contrast with London's grey) (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting and sound designer, explain how you would design the scene in which the company burns the ship's deck to fuel the engines during the Atlantic crossing. Refer to specific lighting and sound choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting choices named and justified: floor-level warm orange flicker to suggest fire (floor lanterns or footlights), contrasted with cool steel-blue wash from above for the night-time Atlantic. Named effect on audience (visual tension between cold ocean and growing fire; desperation communicated without dialogue). Specific sound design: drone beneath the scene representing failing engines; crack and hiss of burning timber; non-diegetic string underscore rising in pitch to signal mounting stakes. Every choice anchored to this specific moment with a named effect on the audience. Design choices work together coherently.

Secure: At least two specific design elements named (one lighting, one sound) with effects. The moment is identified and the design is broadly coherent. Some use of technical vocabulary.

Developing: Design ideas are present but generic (exciting lights, dramatic music). Effects implied but not stated. Little technical vocabulary.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas (fire-coloured lights, sad music) with no justification or effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the playwright's intentions in using minimal scenography rather than a fully realistic set for this production. What is the audience meant to experience and understand?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses multiple intentions: the audience as active co-creators of each location; the theatrical self-awareness of the production (it celebrates storytelling as a craft, not illusion); the ensemble's skill is foregrounded as part of the meaning (watching the transformation is part of the pleasure). Identifies that the form mirrors the adventure's speed and energy: a naturalistic set would require pauses that would drain the pace Verne's narrative demands. Every point anchored to a named moment with a named audience effect. Awareness of the in-the-round configuration's design implications.

Secure: Identifies at least two reasons for the minimal set with generally accurate audience effects. At least one named moment. Some technical vocabulary.

Developing: States that the minimal set 'helps the audience imagine' without developing the idea. Limited reference to specific moments or design choices.

Emerging: Describes that there is not much set without analysing why this was chosen or what the audience experiences as a result.

practice_questions.text: As a director, explain how you would design the staging of the Reform Club opening scene and the transition to the first travel sequence. Cover your set, lighting, sound and costume choices, and explain how each communicates the play's themes of precision and adventure to the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial design across all four disciplines, coherent and specific. Set: minimal furniture (a table, chairs) placed centre stage or on a raised platform; precise geometry of placement mirroring Fogg's world. Lighting: a neutral, slightly cool wash for London; naming of lantern type for the Reform Club interior (profile lanterns from above for formality and precision). Sound: specific soundscape elements (clock ticking, gentlemen's murmur, perhaps a distant foghorn signalling the journey to come). Costume: Fogg's consistent dark, precise base layer versus the ensemble's more varied accessories; the speed of the first role-switch from Club gentleman to customs official or ship's crew. Transition staging: how the lighting and soundscape shift to the first travel location, naming the new lighting wash colour and any specific sound cue. Every choice has a named effect on the audience. Directorial judgement about the overall intended impression (precision, control, the thrill of impending disorder).

Secure: Most disciplines covered with concrete choices. At least one named element per discipline. Some audience effect stated. The transition is acknowledged.

Developing: Some disciplines covered, choices are partly generic. Effects implied. The transition is mentioned but not designed.

Emerging: Basic listing of design ideas for one or two disciplines. Little effect, no transition discussion.

knowledge_checks.q: What staging configuration did the original 2013 production of Around the World in 80 Days use at the New Vic?
In minimal scenography, what primarily substitutes for physical scenery to create location?
A _____ lantern produces a sharp-edged beam used to isolate a performer or moment in a pool of light.
In this production, a warm amber lighting _____ is used to communicate the heat and geography of the India sequence.
Match each design element to its function in this production.
right: Projects a pattern (e.g. water ripples) onto the stage floor to create a location
Non-diegetic music beneath the action to enhance mood unheard by characters
A single accessory that instantly communicates a character's role without a full change

flashcard_questions.q: What is theatre in the round?
flashcard_questions.a: A staging configuration in which the audience surrounds the performance space on all sides.
An approach using as few physical elements as possible, relying on lighting, sound and performance.
A lighting state that covers the whole stage in a single colour or intensity.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a gobo do in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: Projects a pattern or shape onto the stage using a plate placed in front of a lantern.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a profile lantern used for?
flashcard_questions.a: Producing a sharp-edged beam to focus light precisely on a performer or area.
A layered composition of sounds used to create atmosphere or environment in a scene.

flashcard_questions.q: What is underscore in sound design?
flashcard_questions.a: Music or sound beneath the action to enhance mood, unheard by the characters.
The area of the stage furthest from the audience.
The area of the stage closest to the audience.
Using a single accessory to instantly communicate a character's role without a full change.

flashcard_questions.q: What is levels in set design?
flashcard_questions.a: The use of raised or lowered areas to create visual hierarchy and show status.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is in-the-round staging particularly suited to this production?
flashcard_questions.a: It forces minimal scenography and means the ensemble's physical storytelling is visible from all sides.

glossary_terms.definition: A staging configuration in which the audience surrounds the performance space on all sides.
An approach to set design that uses as few physical elements as possible, relying on lighting, sound and performance to create location and atmosphere.
The spatial arrangement of the performance area, including the use of different heights, distances and zones to communicate status, theme or relationship.
The use of raised or lowered areas of the stage — platforms, steps, the floor — to create visual hierarchy and to show status or power.
The area of the stage furthest from the audience.
The area of the stage closest to the audience.
A lighting state that covers the whole stage in a single colour or intensity.
A lantern that produces a sharp-edged beam, used to focus light precisely on a performer or object.
A metal or glass plate placed in front of a lantern to project a pattern onto the stage.
A layered composition of recorded or live sounds used to create an atmosphere or environment in a scene.
Music or sound that plays beneath the action of a scene to enhance mood, unheard by the characters.
A repeating pattern of sound, often below the threshold of conscious hearing, used to create unease or mounting tension.
The practice of using a simple costume piece — a hat, a coat, an accessory — to instantly communicate a character's role, class or nationality without a full costume change.
